units.text: 04. Hume and Kant: the rift between world and mind

Every day we light fires, press switches and cross bridges assuming known regularities will continue. We do not hold a seminar on induction before every gesture. David Hume nevertheless observes something uncomfortable: that a sequence has repeated does not entail, through pure logic, that it must repeat tomorrow (Hume, 1748, sec. IV–V) .

The argument is not that everything will become chaotic tomorrow. It is that the justification ‘it has always worked’ already uses a transfer from past to future. If we justify the transfer by saying such transfers worked in the past, we return to what needed justification. Experience provides extraordinary practical support, but not a deduction making every other future impossible.

Hume thus separates logical certainty from expectation formed through experience. Habit plays a central role in how the mind connects events. I see the first event and expect the second. But where do I see necessity itself? In observation I encounter events and sequences, not a metaphysical force labeled ‘must’ (Hume, 1748, sec. VII) .

This critique does not demolish research. It removes an overly convenient justification. We can seek more robust models, vary conditions, test in new situations and organize confidence by degrees. The philosophical problem of induction remains, but it does not make all forecasts equal. Lacking an absolute guarantee does not mean having no reason.

Imagine two people planning to build a bridge. One uses experiments, calculation and independent checks. The other rolls dice to choose dimensions. Hume does not make them epistemically equivalent. The first person’s inability to prove nature’s eternal uniformity does not erase their advantage relative to the goal. Skepticism becomes confused when it demands of the prudent person an infallibility the imprudent one does not even try to offer.

Kant responds by shifting the question: what conditions make experience of an objective world possible for us? We do not simply receive a ready-organized stream for the mind to photograph. In his view, experience presupposes forms and categories through which objects can be known; causality holds a central place. Knowledge of nature is linked to this contribution of the subject (Kant, 1783, §§14–38; 1781/1787) .

This does not mean individual desire can decide an experiment’s outcome. When Kant discusses the mind’s contribution, he does not claim that each person arbitrarily invents gravity. He examines the general conditions of possible experience. The distinction between such conditions and a law’s empirical content is essential: the structure of knowledge does not by itself supply every equation of physics.

We can formulate the tension through an example. A camera has a sensor selecting part of the light. The photograph depends on the world and the device. Noticing the device’s role does not prove that the photograph shows nothing real. But neither does it allow us to confuse the photograph with the photographed thing in every respect. The analogy has limits: Kant discusses conditions far more fundamental than a technical device. Yet it shows why ‘depends on the mind’ and ‘is arbitrary’ are different propositions.

Later criticism may ask whether certain structures considered necessary are actually revisable. Conceptual progress sometimes forces us to learn ways of thinking that contradict everyday intuition. We need not declare the entire Kantian dispute settled to acknowledge this possibility. But developing a new physical theory does not automatically resolve the philosophical problem of our access to the world either.

Hume prevents us from confusing past success with absolute necessity. Kant prevents us from forgetting the mind’s organizing contribution. Between them opens the space in which we still work: trying to know something independent of our desires with conceptual tools that are not independent of us.

It does not follow that truth is impossible. It follows that a mature picture of knowledge must be able to say two things simultaneously: there is resistance from the world and selection by the mind. Without the first, any story would suffice. Without the second, we would not understand why discovering a law sometimes also means inventing a new way to ask the question.
